phonemes.desc: Short alpha followed by nu; the name opens with a clear, unaspirated 'an'.
Delta-rho-omicron; the root ἀνδρ- means 'man, husband, warrior'.
Long epsilon (eta) with acute [méː] — the pitch peak and a ruler's domain.
Delta-eta, long final syllable; the name ends in the feminine agent suffix.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ahn-dro-MAY-day' — the third syllable is pitched and drawn out; the final -ē is long.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Ἀνδρομέδη (Andromédē), 'she who thinks/ruled like a man' or 'ruler of men'

kin.label: Ethiopian/Phoenician
kin.form: The princess of Aithiopia in most sources; her name is Greek, not local

kin.label: Latin
kin.form: Andromeda, adopted directly into Roman poetry and astronomy

pronunciation.note: Andromédē is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἀνδρομέδη contains both stress (acute on the long η) and length (η). The compound is transparently Greek, though the princess herself is said to dwell in Ethiopia.

domains.title: The Chained Princess
domains.subtitle: Rescue, Constellation, Royal Sacrifice
domains.lead: Andromédē is the princess chained to a sea-rock, offered to a monster and saved by a hero. Her myth is one of the most widely reproduced rescue narratives in Western art, and her catasterism placed her among the stars forever.

cards.name: Royal Daughter
cards.desc: Daughter of Kepheus and Kassiepeia, rulers of Aithiopia; her lineage is royal and unfortunate.

cards.name: Sacrifice to the Sea
cards.desc: Chained to a coastal rock as appeasement to the sea-monster sent by Poseidôn.

cards.name: Perseus's Rescue
cards.desc: Saved by the gorgon-slayer, she becomes his wife and ancestor of Persian kings.

cards.name: Constellation
cards.desc: After death she is placed in the northern sky, the Andromeda galaxy her stellar home.

symbols.name: Sea-rock and chains
symbols.meaning: Her exposure to the ketos and the vulnerability of innocence before power

symbols.name: Mirror of Kassiepeia
symbols.meaning: The boast that set the myth in motion: her mother's claim to surpass the Nereids

symbols.name: Head of Medousa
symbols.meaning: The weapon Perseus carries when he rescues her

symbols.name: Wedding crown
symbols.meaning: Her marriage to Perseus and catasterism into the northern sky

mythology.lead: Andromédē's story is a chain of consequences: a queen's boast, a god's wrath, a daughter's punishment, and a hero's arrival at the decisive moment. It is also a founding myth of genealogy, linking Greek and Persian royal lines.

myths.title: The Boast of Kassiepeia
myths.text: Kassiepeia boasted that she — or her daughter — was more beautiful than the Nereids. Poseidôn, enraged on behalf of his sea-nymphs, sent a flood and a sea-monster (ketos) to ravage Aithiopia. The oracle of Ammon declared that only the sacrifice of Andromédē could appease him.

myths.title: Chained to the Rock
myths.text: Andromédē was stripped and bound to a sea-cliff as the monster approached. The scene became one of the most painted moments in Western art: the maiden's pale body against dark rocks, the hero descending with winged sandals, the creature rising from the foam.

myths.title: The Stars of Andromeda
myths.text: After her death, Athena placed Andromédē in the heavens near Perseus, Kepheus, and Kassiepeia. The constellation preserves the family group in stellar form; the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), visible to the naked eye, bears her name.

lore.syncretism: The Romans adopted Andromeda without renaming her; she is one of the few Greek mythic figures to enter Latin poetry under her original form. In the Middle Ages and Renaissance she became an emblem of rescue, feminine beauty in distress, and the redemptive hero. Modern astronomy keeps her constellation and galaxy names intact. Some scholars compare her Near Eastern analogues — the exposed princess, the sea-monster combat — but the Greek narrative is distinctively tied to Perseus and the Argolid-Persian genealogy.
lore.culturalLegacy: Andromeda is the archetype of the damsel in distress and the catasterized heroine. From Titian and Rubens to Victorian painting and modern fantasy, her image persists: the chained woman, the arriving savior, the monster from the deep. The Andromeda Galaxy, 2.5 million light-years away, carries her name into astrophysics, making her one of the few Greek figures whose cultural reach extends beyond the solar system.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Andromeda is not a willing victim; she is the price of someone else's pride. Her passivity on the rock is not weakness but the consequence of a cosmic transaction in which she had no voice. The myth therefore asks us to look at the people sacrificed to appease forces they did not create.

Yet her rescue is also the myth's redemption. Perseus does not merely slay the monster; he sees her, chooses her, and makes her his equal in marriage. In that moment, the object of sacrifice becomes a queen and a star. Andromeda reminds us that dignity can survive exposure, and that the gaze that recognizes suffering can also transform it.
lore.archaeology: The myth of Andromeda was popular in Greek and Roman visual culture. Painted vases show Perseus approaching the chained maiden; Roman wall paintings and sarcophagi reproduce the rescue scene. The constellation was mapped by Ptolemy and transmitted through Arabic and Renaissance star catalogs. No single archaeological site claims to be her rock, though Joppa (modern Jaffa) was identified with the location in antiquity.
